extracted.intended_audience: readers of political economy; manufacturers and policymakers (students, industrialists, and statesmen)
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and breakdown of the discrete processes in pin manufacture and the broader principles of the division of labour, with time, wage, cost, and organisation implications; includes comparison between hand labour and a pin-making machine and an account of dividing large computational tasks. Useful for analysing manufacturing efficiency and organisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawing Wire
rubrics_metrics.description: The initial process of producing the wire from which pins are made (listed as process 1 in the analysis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented in the tabular analysis with time, cost of making 1 lb of pins, and earnings per day for the workman; used as a discrete operation whose time and wage contribute to total cost of a manufactured pound of pins. (See table entries for the English manufacture.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Straightening and Cutting the Wire
rubrics_metrics.description: The operation of straightening the drawn wire and cutting it to length (listed among the elementary processes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given as a separate process in the tabular breakdown with its own time-cost and typical wages for women/girls; treated as a unit of work whose cost should be separately measured when analysing manufacture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pointing
rubrics_metrics.description: The process of forming the pointed end of the pin (coarse and fine pointing stages are discussed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as a distinct operation with substantial time and high wages relative to some other processes (pointing can command higher pay); table quantifies time/cost and shows pointing productivity differences between machine and hand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twisting and Cutting the Heads (Turning the Spiral & Cutting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Process of producing the spiral for heads and cutting off the heads from the spiral coil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained as a separate operation with specific pay-rates for boys and men and measured output per day; part of the sequential chain of operations whose separate cost and time are tabulated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heading
rubrics_metrics.description: Fixing the head on the body of the pin using a stake and die (process usually executed by women and children).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed operation: stake with cavity, die lifted by pedal, groove to admit pin body, three or four blows on circumference, hammer 7–10 lb falling 1–2 inches; spoilage ~1% reserved for melting-pot; dies require repair after ~30 pounds of pins. Wages and daily outputs provided (e.g., 1s.6d. per 20,000; skilled operator 10–20k/day). These operational details affect cost, quality, and die-wear estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tinning (Whitening)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cleaning and covering pins with tin (pickle, tartar solution with tin grains, boiling, bran washing and drying).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described step-by-step: pickling to remove grease and roughen surface, boiling ~2½ hours in tartar solution with tin grains, washing in bran, shaking in dry bran to dry; batch size typically 56 lb; pay typically one penny per pound for the worker; typical earnings and assistant costs are noted. These process parameters determine throughput, labour allocation (worker dries previous batch while boiling), and unit cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Papering
rubrics_metrics.description: Arranging pins side by side into paper (usually performed by women).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: use of comb to align pins, fixing between iron pieces with grooves, folding paper and pressing against points so pins pass through folds; wages indicated (about 1s.6d. per day for women; children earn less). Treated as a final discrete process with measurable time/cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tabular analysis of time, cost, and earnings per process
rubrics_metrics.description: Presenting a tabular view of the time occupied by each process, its cost, and the sums which can be earned by persons confined solely to each process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tabulated breakdown (English and French manufacture examples) to compute total labour-time, cost of making a pound/dozen of pins, cost-per-part (even given as millionths of a penny), number of persons employed, and compare national manufacturing systems. The table is used to illustrate how division of labour reduces cost and to assess wage/skill relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine evaluation — defects of machine-made pins
rubrics_metrics.description: To judge a machine's value one must inquire 'To what defects pins so made are liable?' (i.e., what quality defects the machine product exhibits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text notes machine-made pins may be more likely to bend because heads are punched from solid wire which should be soft; annealing trade-offs (softening head-end vs body strength) and possible remedies (spin heads and fix them, or anneal only head end) are discussed. Use this question to assess quality risks and necessary process adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine evaluation — advantages of machine-made pins
rubrics_metrics.description: To judge a machine's value one must inquire 'What advantages they possess over those made in the usual way?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes machine pins can be better in some respects (e.g., less likely to lose heads). This criterion asks to identify tangible quality or consistency improvements a machine delivers compared with hand labour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine evaluation — prime cost of a machine
rubrics_metrics.description: To judge a machine's value one must inquire 'What is the prime cost of a machine for making them?' (capital cost).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prime cost per unit falls if many machines/numbers are required; factor into unit cost calculations and capital amortisation when comparing to hand labour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine evaluation — expense of keeping it in repair
rubrics_metrics.description: To judge a machine's value one must inquire 'What is the expense of keeping it in repair?' (maintenance/wear-and-tear).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text observes dies/clams will wear quickly unless wire softened by annealing; repair/wear rates depend on material hardness and process choices. Include expected maintenance intervals and replacement parts in cost models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine evaluation — expense of moving and attending it
rubrics_metrics.description: To judge a machine's value one must inquire 'What is the expense of moving it and attending to it?' (operational labour and logistics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider staffing needed to operate the machine (often one labourer), costs of moving/installing/transporting, and attendant labor; although machines centralise many tasks, they require attendants and logistical costs that influence the overall economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess trade-offs between machine and hand production
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare machine and human labour in speed, quality, and labour requirements (e.g., machine makes ~60 pins per minute; machine pointing 3,600/hour vs man 15,600/hour; machine heading 2.5x faster).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate both throughput and qualitative trade-offs: machines may be slower in some processes and faster in others; consider force requirements (a machine may reduce physical labour), the ability for one attendant to run many processes at once, and effects on product defects and rework rates when deciding adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle: match skill to process (advantage increases with high-skill/short-duration tasks)
rubrics_metrics.description: The higher the skill required for a process and the smaller the fraction of time it occupies in producing the whole, the greater the advantage of separating that process and dedicating a specialised workman to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured by wages earned in specialised tasks; if one person had to perform all processes he would need to be paid at the higher rates appropriate for the most skilled stages, substantially increasing total cost. Use wage differentials and time shares to decide whether to subdivide tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability condition for division of labour
rubrics_metrics.description: Division of labour cannot be successfully practised unless there exists a great demand for its produce and it requires larger capital to be employed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use market demand and capital availability as preconditions when planning subdivision and specialisation; example: watchmaking requires many specialised branches and capital to apply the principle economically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organisation of large computational work by division of mental labour (Prony's three sections)
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide mental/computational enterprises into: first section (analysts to derive formulae and suitable expressions), second section (experienced mathematicians to convert formulae into numeric instructions and perform verification), third section (many low-skilled computers performing simple additions/subtractions to produce tables).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First section handles theoretical selection of formulae, second section performs conversions and provides verification means so third section's mechanical work needn't be rechecked in full. The model shows how complex intellectual tasks can be organised to economise highly skilled labour and to scale up production using low-skilled workers; anticipate that machinery may later replace the third section and shift attention of analysts to simplification of conversions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need to know separate cost of each process and wear-and-tear
rubrics_metrics.description: Producers, distributors, and statesmen should know the precise expense of every process and the wear-and-tear of machinery due to each process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This knowledge enables producers to discover improved cost-reducing methods, distributors to explain prices or suggest fashion changes, and statesmen to judge tax impacts accurately. It is a strategic diagnostic tool for economic decision-making and policy.
